rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The phrase may refer to Adam and Eve.
rows.anchor: From a male and a female can be understood as a reference to Adam and Eve (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, it refers to each human being's creation from the fluids of a man and a woman.
rows.anchor: but also to the creation of each human being from the fluid of a man and a woman (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Differences in tribe, race, ethnicity, language, nationality, and religion can help people appreciate the reality of the human condition.
rows.anchor: That people have been divided into diverse peoples and tribes that they may come to know one another indicates the manner

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says God judges people by their hearts, not by their bodies or outward forms.
rows.anchor: In this regard, the Prophet has said, “God does not look at your bodies, nor at your forms. He looks at your hearts.”

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A cited hadith presents the heart as determining the whole body's state: purity of heart purifies the body, while pollution corrupts it.
rows.anchor: In another ḥadīth, the heart is presented as the reality that determines all other dimensions of one’s being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human diversity is among the greatest worldly tests; 5:48 says God made people diverse to test them and directs them to compete in good deeds before returning to Him.
rows.anchor: as in 5:48: And had God willed, He would have made you one community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā means reverence, God-fearing, or simply fearing in pre-Islamic usage.
rows.anchor: has the sense of “God-fearing,” or just “fearing” in pre-Islamic Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This late Madinan verse recasts Arabia's moral order: true worth rests on faith and piety rather than lineage or displays of valor and generosity, once treated as opposites to reverence.
rows.anchor: This late Madinan verse thus signals a revamping of the moral order of Arabia to one in which true worth is no longer determined by lineage

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly said Islam removed jāhiliyyah zealotry and boasting of descent: all people descend from Adam, and the most beloved to God at Resurrection are the most obedient and reverent.
rows.anchor: In this vein, the Prophet is reported to have said, “Truly God has ennobled those who were lowly during the Age of Ignorance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-insān means man or the human being as such.
rows.anchor: Man translates al-insān, which also means the human being as such.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some understand the human being as Adam and the verse as God's knowledge of his inclination to eat what was forbidden.
rows.anchor: some understand it as a reference to Adam and God’s knowledge of his inclination to eat of what had been forbidden to him (Q)

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most take the phrase to mean that God knows what lies within people and the true intentions behind their words and actions, even when they themselves are unaware.
rows.anchor: Most, however, see it as a reference to God’s Knowledge of all that lies within breasts

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: An alternative reading takes the phrase to say that God knows what the soul whispers.
rows.anchor: The second phrase could also be read, “and We know that of which his soul whispers” (Aj).

words: وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many commentators find the statement of nearness problematic and seek to avoid its literal meaning.
rows.anchor: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein is problematic for many commentators.

words: وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ
rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some commentators say “We” refers to the two angels, thereby avoiding a literal reading of divine nearness.
rows.anchor: Some seek to avoid the literal meaning, saying that “we” refers to two angels (IK).

words: وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ
rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Others connect the phrase to the next verse: God's nearness holds when the two receivers arrive, and He remains powerful over them and needs no angels to know human actions.
rows.anchor: He is not in need of them in order to know what the person is doing (Z).

words: وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author sees the verse as affirming God's immanence throughout creation: Divine Reality underlies every reality and is nearest to each human being; God is with people wherever they are.
rows.anchor: this is one of several verses that indicate the Immanence of God in all of creation (see, e.g., 2:115)

words: وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ ٱلْوَرِيدِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although God is always close, people often fail to be close to Him and so remain far away.
rows.anchor: human beings, nonetheless, often fail to be with or close to God and thus remain far from Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the meaning of “his companion,” the commentary directs readers to 50:23.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of his companion, see 50:23c.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The companion declares himself innocent of the person's actions.
rows.anchor: I did not make him rebel declares the companion’s innocence of what the person does (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disclaimer resembles Satan's declaration that he is quit of those who followed his call to disbelief and that he fears God.
rows.anchor: as when Satan says to human beings after they have followed his injunction to disbelieve, Surely I am quit of you. Truly I fear God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan elsewhere says he had no authority over people, only called them and they responded, so they should blame themselves.
rows.anchor: when Satan declares, I had no authority over you, save that I called you, and you responded to me.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These passages show that people bear responsibility for their souls; they would not heed Satan's suggestions if they were not already far astray.
rows.anchor: Such verses indicate that all human beings bear responsibility for the state of their soul and would not incline to suggestions from Satan

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators agree that al-Ṭūr is Makkan, most likely from the latter half of the Makkan period.
rows.anchor: commentators agree that al-Ṭūr is from the Makkan period, most likely from the latter half.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say Sūrah al-Ṭūr was revealed immediately after Sūrah 32, al-Sajdah.
rows.anchor: According to some it was revealed immediately after Sūrah 32, al-Sajdah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the Mount mentioned in its first verse; most understand al-Ṭūr as Mount Sinai wherever it appears in the Quran, while the full name occurs in 23:20 and 95:2.
rows.anchor: name from the mention of the Mount

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening half follows Sūrah 51 by treating the promised Day (51:60) and punishment for its wrongdoers and disbelievers (51:59–60); the sūrah affirms that promise (51:5, 51:22) and further warns of it.
rows.anchor: the first half (vv. 1–28) focuses upon the subject of the concluding verse of that sūrah, the Day that they are promised (51:60

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah begins with oaths and the coming punishment and Judgment, contrasts the deniers' fate with the reverent's reward, answers accusations against the Prophet, challenges deniers, and ends by counseling patience and praise of God.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭūr begins with a series of oaths and a promise of God’s impending punishment and the Day of Judgment (vv. 1–10)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Idle talk is often vain discussion but more broadly means becoming engrossed in worldly vanities.
rows.anchor: To play in idle talk is often associated with vain discussion (6:68; see 6:68–69c), but it means more generally to become engrossed with the vanities of this world (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase has become an idiomatic Arabic expression; the commentary refers readers to its discussion at 70:42 and 74:45.
rows.anchor: Regarding the meaning of this verse, which has become an idiomatic Arabic expression, see 70:42c; 74:45c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several Quranic passages directly connect denying God with idle talk.
rows.anchor: Several Quranic passages indicate a direct connection between denying God and idle talk.

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet promises the Garden to whoever guarantees control of what lies between the lips and thighs.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth: “Whosoever can guarantee me that he will control what is between his two lips and his two thighs, I will guarantee him the Garden.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that the tongue's fornication is an enticing word.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is also reported to have said, “The fornication of the tongue is the enticing word.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When teaching Muʿādh ibn Jabal, the Prophet held his tongue and warned that tongue jests drag people into the Fire; Muʿādh had asked whether speech is accountable.
rows.anchor: when the Prophet instructed the prominent Companion Muʿādh ibn Jabal in the principles of Islam, he took hold of his own tongue and said, “Restrain this.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers are graphically described as violently cast into Hell, dragged on their faces, shackled, and given boiling liquid and cold, murky fluid.
rows.anchor: The violent way the deniers are cast into the Fire is described graphically in many verses: they are dragged upon their faces (54:48)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: An alternative reading says they are called unto Hell with a great calling.
rows.anchor: This verse could also be read, “a day when they are called unto the Fire of Hell with a [great] calling” (Bḍ).

words: هَٰذِهِ ٱلنَّارُ ٱلَّتِى كُنتُم بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse is comparable to 83:17 and resembles 77:29.
rows.anchor: Cf. 83:17. This verse is similar to 77:29: Away to that which you used to deny!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 14–16 are understood as words spoken by angels to the inhabitants of the Fire.
rows.anchor: Vv. 14–16 are understood to be uttered by the angels to the inhabitants of the Fire.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your companion” refers to the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Your companion refers to the Prophet Muhammad.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take ḍalla, being astray, as the opposite of guidance (hudā).
rows.anchor: Some maintain that“to be astray” or “to stray” (ḍalla

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R identifies ghawā, to err, as the opposite of sound judgment (rushd); R is also cited among those explaining erring as ignorance from adherence to corrupt creed.
rows.anchor: err” is also understood to indicate ignorance that results from adhering to a corrupt creed (Iṣ, R, Ṭb).

rows.speaker: Iṣ, R, Ṭb
rows.claim: Other commentators understand erring as ignorance caused by adherence to a corrupt creed.
rows.anchor: “To err” is also understood to indicate ignorance that results from adhering to a corrupt creed (Iṣ, R, Ṭb).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this distinction, straying is lack of guidance, while erring is following religion incorrectly.
rows.anchor: In this sense, “to be astray” indicates the absence of guidance, while “to err” indicates that one is mistaken in how one follows religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Caprice (hawā) opposes guidance and truth: one follows God and His messengers or one's own inclinations; see 45:23.
rows.anchor: important Quranic concept, often placed in direct opposition to guidance and truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's lack of caprice means he did not author revelation and his own speech is guided; together, the claims affirm true religion, correct practice, and freedom from whim.
rows.anchor: That the Prophet does not speak out of caprice indicates both that he did not author the revelation himself and that his own speech is guided.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the one of awesome power as the Archangel Gabriel, who imparted revelation to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: The one of awesome power is understood by most commentators to be a reference to the Archangel Gabriel, who imparted the revelation to the Prophet (JJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators identify the one of awesome power as God Himself.
rows.anchor: and by others as a reference to God Himself.

rows.speaker: JJ, Q, Ṭb
rows.claim: One view is that Gabriel revealed to the Prophet, God's servant, what God had revealed to Gabriel.
rows.anchor: (JJ, Q, Ṭb), in which case it would be rendered,“Then he revealed to his servant what he revealed”

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭb
rows.claim: A second view is that God revealed the revelation directly to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: that God revealed the revelation directly to the Prophet (Q, Ṭb)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view is that God revealed to Gabriel, His servant, what Gabriel later transmitted to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: what Gabriel then transmitted to the Prophet.

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭb
rows.claim: The revelation's content is left unnamed to honor its exalted status.
rows.anchor: What is revealed is not mentioned by name out of reverence for its exalted status (JJ, Ṭb).

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The verse may refer either to the Prophet seeing Gabriel in his true form twice or to two distinct visions of God.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to either the two times in which the Prophet is said to have seen Gabriel in his true form or two separate visions of God (Aj).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is said to have seen Gabriel's true form twice: at Mount Ḥirāʾ during the first revelation and again during the Ascension.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is said to have seen Gabriel’s true form only twice, once at Mount Ḥirāʾ, where he received the first revelation, and a second time during the Ascension.

rows.speaker: those who maintain the vision of God
rows.claim: Proponents of the God-vision interpretation say the Prophet saw his Lord twice in special Self-Disclosure: above the Throne at the highest veil and at the Lote Tree of the Boundary.
rows.anchor: Those who maintain that it refers to the vision of God say that the Prophet saw his Lord twice in a special Self-Disclosure
